source: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Class X Political Science), Chapter 5

overview.bigIdea: Democracy is **just a form of government** – it creates conditions; citizens must use them. Judge it fairly: it is clearly better at **legitimacy, dignity and handling diversity**; its record on **growth, inequality and corruption** is mixed.

ladder.a: Legitimate – yes; responsive and clean – mixed

lessons.title: Accountable, responsive and legitimate government
lessons.hook: Nannu, a daily-wage earner, waited three months for a duplicate ration card. Then he filed an application under the **Right to Information Act** – and within a week the officials came to him. That is what an **accountable** government looks like.

core.def: Promotes equality · enhances dignity · improves decision making · resolves conflicts · allows room to correct mistakes.
People choose and control their rulers; government answers to citizens and responds to their needs.
A citizen has the right and means to examine the process of decision making – often missing in non-democracies.
Democracy may be slow, less efficient, not always responsive or clean – but it is people’s own government.
Good at regular free elections and open public debate; weak at sharing information, responsiveness and freedom from corruption.

explain: Democracy is slower because it is based on **deliberation and negotiation** – but decisions that follow procedures are more acceptable and effective. ‘The cost of time that democracy pays is perhaps worth it.’
Surveys in South Asia show overwhelming support for democracy – even in countries without democratic regimes. Democracy’s ability to generate its own support is itself an outcome.

example.q: How does democracy produce an accountable, responsive and legitimate government? (5 marks)
steps: **Elections:** regular, free and fair elections let people choose and change their rulers.
**Public debate:** open debate on major policies and laws lets citizens take part in decisions.
**Right to information / transparency:** citizens can examine how decisions are made – e.g. Nannu’s RTI application.
**Procedures:** decisions follow norms and procedures, so they are more acceptable even if slower.
**Legitimacy:** it is people’s own government, which is why support for democracy is overwhelming.

mistakes: Claiming democracies are free of corruption.
Saying slowness makes democracy worse without explaining the benefit.
Forgetting ‘legitimacy’ – the one area where democracy is certainly better.
lessons.tip: In outcome answers, always add one sentence on the weakness too – examiners reward balanced answers.

lessons.title: Economic growth, inequality and poverty
lessons.hook: If democracy produces good government, shouldn’t it also make countries richer and fairer? The evidence surprises many students: **dictatorships grew slightly faster**, and many democracies remain very unequal.

core.def: All democracies 3.95% · all dictatorships 4.42% · poor countries under dictatorship 4.34% · poor countries under democracy 4.28%.
Democracy is not a guarantee of economic development – but we can expect it not to lag behind dictatorships; the difference in poor countries is negligible.
Depends on population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries, economic priorities, etc.
South Africa and Brazil: top 20% take more than 60% of income, bottom 20% less than 3%. Denmark and Hungary are much more equal.
The poor are a large share of voters, yet governments are not as keen on poverty as expected; in Bangladesh more than half live in poverty.

explain: Democracies are based on **political equality** (one person, one vote), but economic inequality has grown: a small number of ultra-rich take a highly disproportionate share of wealth and income.
When the growth difference is so small, it is better to prefer democracy because it has several other positive outcomes.

example.q: ‘Democracy cannot reduce inequality of incomes.’ Give arguments for and against. (5 marks)
steps: **For:** in democracies like South Africa and Brazil the top 20% take over 60% of national income while the bottom 20% get under 3%.
**For:** the share of the ultra-rich has been increasing while incomes at the bottom decline; the poor struggle to meet basic needs.
**For:** elected governments are not as keen to address poverty as expected (e.g. Bangladesh).
**Against:** some democracies like Denmark and Hungary have much more equal distribution.
**Against:** political equality gives the poor a vote and voice to demand welfare; democracy is still preferred for its other outcomes.
example.answer: Arguments on both sides with Table 2 evidence.

mistakes: Mixing up the table numbers (4.42 is dictatorships).
Forgetting that the difference among poor countries is negligible.
lessons.tip: Quote ONE number per claim – ‘3.95% vs 4.42%’ or ‘top 20% take 64.8% in South Africa’ – it makes the answer authoritative.
lessons.memory: Growth: dictatorship slightly ahead (4.42 vs 3.95). Poor countries: almost equal (4.34 vs 4.28).

lessons.title: Social diversity, dignity and freedom
lessons.hook: Belgium negotiated its differences; Sri Lanka did not. Democracy cannot make conflicts vanish, but it gives a **peaceful way to handle them** – and it treats every person with dignity, at least in principle.

core.def: Democracies develop procedures to conduct competition, reducing the chance of explosive or violent tensions; non-democracies often suppress differences.
Democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion: the majority must work with the minority; majority and minority opinions are not permanent.
Rule by majority must not become rule by the majority community (religion, race, language). Every citizen must have a chance of being in the majority at some time.
Democracy is far superior in promoting individual dignity and freedom – e.g. women’s struggles for equal treatment, and claims of disadvantaged castes for equal status.
As democracy passes one test, it faces another; complaints show people have become citizens, not subjects.

explain: Once equality is recognised in principle, it becomes easier to fight discrimination: caste inequalities and atrocities still happen, but they **lack moral and legal foundations**.
‘The fact that people are complaining is itself a testimony to the success of democracy.’

example.q: What are the conditions under which democracies accommodate social diversities? (3 marks)
steps: Democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion – the majority must work with the minority so that governments represent the general view.
Rule by majority must not become rule by a majority community based on religion, race or language.
Every citizen must have a chance of being in the majority at some point; if someone is barred from it by birth, democracy stops being accommodative (e.g. Sri Lanka).
example.answer: Work with minority · not majority community · chance to be in majority.

mistakes: Treating ‘majority rule’ as the essence of democracy.
lessons.tip: End any outcomes answer with the line: ‘Democracy transforms people from subjects into citizens.’
lessons.memory: Majority must be temporary, not a community.

revision: Democracy is just a form of government: it creates conditions; citizens must use them.
Expected: accountable, responsive, legitimate government; transparency; regular free elections, open debate, right to information.
Democracy is slower (deliberation) but decisions are more acceptable; it is certainly better at legitimacy.
Record is mixed on responsiveness, sharing information and corruption.
Growth 1950–2000: democracies 3.95%, dictatorships 4.42%; poor countries 4.28% vs 4.34% – negligible difference.
Inequality is high in some democracies (South Africa, Brazil: top 20% >60%); Denmark and Hungary more equal.
Poverty persists though the poor are a large share of voters; Bangladesh: more than half poor.
Accommodating diversity: majority works with minority; majority not a community of religion/race/language.
Democracy promotes dignity and freedom (women, disadvantaged castes).
Complaints show success: people move from subjects to citizens; ‘examination never gets over’.

sections.title: Outcome answers · 4 steps
items: State the expectation (e.g. democracy should reduce inequality).
Give the evidence (table, survey, example).
Judge: does democracy do well or not?
Conclude with why democracy is still preferred.

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line definition or introduction using textbook keywords (e.g. ‘Majoritarianism is …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, with the key term in the first few words. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a real example from the chapter to each point (Belgium, Sri Lanka, Panchayati Raj, a party, a survey figure).
Use the exact numbers the textbook gives only when you are sure (59%, 1956, 1992, one-third, 1976).
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ questions use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Distinguish’ questions draw a small two-column table.
Case-based questions: underline the key line in the passage first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn sorts – if you can sort every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can explain accountable, responsive and legitimate government with transparency and RTI.
I can quote Table 1 growth rates and explain the conclusion.
I can use Table 2 to discuss inequality.
I can state the two conditions for accommodating diversity.
I can explain how democracy promotes dignity and why complaints show success.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark case/source-based and 5-mark long answers). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
